cards.headline:
Vercel Agent asks before
it changes production
cards.body: Vercel Agent investigates with read-only access, then needs a user to approve its plan before making changes.

blocks.x: A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t say upfront which actions an agent will take or what access it needs. Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out.

blocks.cap: How a deployment request becomes a plan with permissions.

blocks.x: For a broken deployment, it might inspect build logs and compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one under read-only scopes, which run automatically. A proposed redeploy requests read-write:deployment access in a plan the user approves in one decision.

blocks.cap: How Vercel Agent gets a token for approved work.

blocks.x: Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have. The OAuth service issues shorter-lived scoped tokens, and Vercel APIs reject operations outside them, even if the model considers the action necessary.

blocks.cap: What happens when a plan is approved, rejected, or stopped.

blocks.x: Before resuming work, the runtime checks that the plan is still active; a stopped plan fails even if its token hasn’t expired. Scoped credentials work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits and audit logs.
